prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength opened the regime of 10^-18 precision in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B012, a single-part prize to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After the full round-1 exchange, five of eight members hold this position for the same reason I do, and what persuades me is the evidence rather than the count. The magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between atom number and Doppler and recoil shifts, so thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated at once with the light shift cancelled. Systematic uncertainty near 1e-18 has been demonstrated and compared between independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL), including over fibre links, and that is the quantitative, repeated demonstration I trust. The chair asks Lindroth and me to say plainly whether Ye's place is justified. It is. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstrations. Ye's group at JILA then took the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability, carried out the cross-clock and frequency-comb comparisons, and used the many-atom ensemble to study density and interaction shifts. Together these made the 1e-18 regime real and credible. I also drop my round-1 suggestion that the first demonstrations and the many-body clock work might need separate wording. The citation can say 'invention and development of the optical lattice clock' and cover both without naming sub-results, since both people hold documented parts of the same chain from idea to record performance.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 (Hall, Haensch) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche) prizes remains the real objection, and I do not think it is fully answerable by argument; the committee has to judge it. My answer is that the comb is a ruler the clock uses and ion control is a different platform: neither prize covers the many-atom neutral lattice at the magic wavelength, which is what produced the order-of-magnitude gain. The citation must name the lattice and not read as a general clock prize. The second objection is early-developer credit (Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto, Ludlow). With a limit of three names and a two-name core on which every member who ranked it agrees, I see no priority claim strong enough to displace Katori or Ye, and a third name would dilute a clean attribution. I would admit the omission openly as a limit of the statutes. The third is the redefinition of the second, which I treat as a consequence of the discovery rather than a precondition, and I return to it in the uncertainties.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the lattice clock is the third prize in one metrology neighbourhood (comb 2005, ion control 2012) and an incremental step in precision, weighing against it when a new state of matter is available, and that the redefinition of the second has not happened.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and it is the objection that could move me, but I read the record differently. The 2005 prize honoured the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems. Neither delivered the neutral-atom lattice that gives both a large atom number and freedom from Doppler and recoil shifts, which is where the order-of-magnitude gain came from. Counting prizes in a neighbourhood is a weaker test than asking whether the capability is new, and a clock at 1e-18 with millimetre-scale redshift sensitivity is a capability that did not exist before. I do not make the prize depend on the redefinition: the SI decision follows from agreed comparisons that already exist. Where I agree with him is that twisted bilayer graphene is a serious candidate and he is right that a new state of matter counts for much; I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that what needs to be stable is the discovery, not the mechanism, since cuprate superconductivity was honoured before its mechanism was understood, and that a new state of matter outweighs a measurement technique.
responses.response: The cuprate comparison is a fair one and I accept that an unresolved pairing mechanism is not by itself disqualifying. My residual concern is narrower: the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes depend on twist-angle homogeneity, and sample-to-sample variation makes the experimental claim harder to pin to a single reproducible measurement, whereas the clock comparisons are repeated numbers between laboratories. I do not accept the distinction that a technique ranks below a state of matter. The statutes speak of a discovery or an invention, and a new measurement regime that opens redshift geodesy, constant drifts and dark-matter searches is both. I would also note that B042 leaves Yuan Cao outside the three names, which is a credit gap larger than anything on B012. I have kept B042 as an alternative and would not consider a B042 prize wrong.

responses.point: Mehlig regards the magic-angle flat band as a stable, parameter-free principle tested by experiment, calls the clock an increment on the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and says he would be comfortable with B012 as the preferred prize.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald model is a clean, transparent result, and I accept that it counts as a principle in a way a measurement technique does not always. Still, the clock is not just an increment in precision: removing the atom-number versus Doppler and recoil trade-off is a physical principle, and the magic wavelength is its sharp, testable condition, confirmed in many laboratories. Where we differ is mainly maturity and credit. The experiment, not the model, is the part that is still debated, and the allocation of two theory names and one experimental name leaves the first author outside, as he himself notes. I am glad he is comfortable with B012, and I answer the chair's question by saying that I would rank B012 above B042 on those grounds and what would move me toward B042 is a settled account of the superconducting state or experimental reproducibility that is not tied to twist-angle control.

responses.point: Lindroth holds the clock first, wants the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice so it does not read as a general clock prize, and says she may over-weight her own field.
responses.response: I agree with her on the citation and have changed the wording to name the lattice and the magic wavelength explicitly. As asked, I will state my own view of the Ye question: his contribution is distinct from the comb work he built on, since the comb is the link between optical and microwave frequencies and his main contribution is the neutral-atom lattice clock performance, including the strontium clock's record accuracy and the density-shift work. I also accept her challenge to test her field-specific enthusiasm. I come at this from an experimental quantum optics background and not from precision metrology, and my reasons are the cross-laboratory comparisons and not familiarity with the field, which is why I am comfortable that the case holds from outside the specialist community.

responses.point: Johansson has moved from circuit QED to the clock and says the Academy would not want two superconducting-circuit prizes within a year or two, so he would not push B005 against that concern.
responses.response: I appreciate the clarification that cQED is a different discovery from the 2025 prize. His reading of the timing concern matches mine and I would leave B005 out this year. I also confirm my deferral on B005: it is in his field and in the field of WACQT, which we both are part of, so I would not argue for or against it. On the chair's question of whether B005 should stay in discussion, no point is unresolved that would change my configuration. On B020 I keep it as a second alternative, but I accept Lindroth's point that its overlap with the 2012 prize is larger than for the clock.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the neutral-atom lattice at the magic wavelength as a distinct achievement from the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes; this is a judgement and not a measurement, and colleagues like Danielsson and Mehlig disagree in good faith.
Whether leaving out Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto and Ludlow is acceptable under the three-name limit; I think it is, but a reader of the literature could reasonably want a wider credit.

Whether the redefinition of the second is treated as precondition or consequence. I treat it as a consequence, because the comparisons that the redefinition rests on already exist, but a more cautious committee might prefer to wait.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene would move ahead of the clock if the superconducting mechanism and sample reproducibility are resolved, which could happen within a few years.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B012: I have no tie to Katori or Ye and have not collaborated with them. My own work on rare-earth-doped crystals and slow-light laser stabilisation is adjacent to frequency stabilisation but is not a collaboration or a competing claim. I lead part of WACQT, which is Chalmers-led and overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home, and circuit QED (B005) is in that field; B005 is not in my configuration and I would defer to Johansson on it. I also have a spin-off company interest (Deep Light Vision) that is unrelated to any shortlisted ballot.
